THOUGHT: This patient has a lifelong, familial, acrally-predominant blistering disorder with nail involvement and no mucosal disease. Onset in childhood with father and brother affected points strongly to an inherited disorder with autosomal dominant transmission. The clinical pattern (hands/feet/legs, nail dystrophy, spontaneous tense bullae/erosions) is most typical of the epidermolysis bullosa (EB) spectrum. Within EB, epidermolysis bullosa simplex (EBS, keratin 5/14 defects) commonly presents in childhood with acral blistering, nail changes, and usually spares mucosa — making it the single most likely diagnosis. Dominant dystrophic EB (COL7A1) is the next most likely inherited alternative (also familial, nail dystrophy, acral blistering) but often has more scarring/milia and can have more severe nail loss. Acquired/subepidermal autoimmune disorders that produce acral blisters (epidermolysis bullosa acquisita, bullous pemphigoid) can mimic inherited EB in adults but are less likely given the lifelong family history and childhood onset. Porphyria cutanea tarda causes photosensitive acral blisters on the dorsal hands and fragile skin, but typically has adult onset, characteristic urine/porphyrin findings and photosensitivity — less consistent with childhood disease and familial occurrence. The case notes that a prior biopsy “confirmed the diagnosis” (though details are not given), which further supports an EB diagnosis rather than an autoimmune or porphyrin disorder.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Epidermolysis bullosa simplex (autosomal dominant EBS)  
2. Dominant dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (DEB)  
3. Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (acquired anti–type VII collagen blistering)  
4. Porphyria cutanea tarda (photosensitive acral blistering)  
5. Bullous pemphigoid (subepidermal autoimmune blistering disease)
